title: Test-Day Patterns
intro: Use a clear routine to answer, check, and move on.

sections.heading: The cut test
body: Test DELETE by reading what remains. Removing an extra verb can leave a describing phrase: “a banner strung across the street.” Removing “it was” can leave a phrase that renames a noun: “an oak, the oldest tree.”
It can also remove an irrelevant or mismatched aside. Keep the cut only if the sentence retains its main verb, subject, and needed meaning.
Before cutting a verb, locate its subject, which can follow it: Beyond the doorway stands a guard.

examples.text: A banner strung across Main Street announces the harvest festival. (after cutting 'was')
examples.label: the broken clause becomes a participial phrase

examples.text: He pointed to an oak, the oldest tree in the county. (after cutting 'it was')
examples.label: the comma splice becomes an appositive

examples.text: The ledger, kept in the captain's own hand, the cargo of every voyage. (after cutting 'lists')
examples.label: this cut removed the only main verb and left a fragment

examples.text: Beside the loading bay stands a crane that moves the largest crates.
examples.label: The inverted subject crane is singular; stands agrees with it and must remain as the main verb.

sections.tip: Read the sentence with the underlined words gone. Complete and cleaner: cut. Missing a subject or verb: trap.

sections.heading: Don't fear NO CHANGE
body: Judge NO CHANGE by the same grammar, meaning, and purpose checks as every alternative. Identify a specific improvement before replacing it.
Comma + but or so can already join two complete thoughts. Replacing that word with however or nevertheless between commas can leave two sentences joined by only commas, creating a comma splice.
Use but for contrast, so for a result, and still for an unexpected outcome in a new sentence.

examples.text: The trail is short, but the climb is steep.
examples.label: comma + 'but' joins the clauses correctly. Keep it.

examples.text: The trail is short, nevertheless, the climb is steep.
examples.label: a conjunctive adverb between commas creates a comma splice

sections.tip: NO CHANGE needs evidence too: check correctness, meaning, and the question’s goal. 'It sounds plain' is not an error.

sections.heading: Read the goal like a contract
body: Break the goal into requirements. If it asks which instruments were built and what they were made from, the choice must answer both.
Check each requirement against the actual wording. A specific, vivid choice that meets only one requirement still fails.
For a formal passage, keep precise factual wording and remove a conversational reaction that the task does not call for.

examples.text: Goal: name which trees were planted and where. 'sugar maples and river birches along the south fence line'
examples.label: names the trees and the place. Both boxes checked.

examples.text: Goal: name which trees were planted and where. 'sugar maples and river birches that arrived as bare-root saplings'
examples.label: names the trees, skips the place. One box. Trap.

examples.text: Formal report: “The second trial reduced the error rate.” Reject “The second trial totally crushed the problem.”
examples.label: The first states a measured result; the casual exaggeration changes the report’s register and certainty.

sections.tip: Count the requirements in the question. The right answer proves every one; the tempting wrong answer proves one.

sections.heading: Point the modifier
body: Identify what the modifier must describe, then test each offered position in the complete sentence.
Put the modifier close to its target without splitting another phrase. Watch only, almost, and nearly: their placement changes what the sentence limits.

examples.text: She packed sandwiches wrapped in foil for the hikers.
examples.label: 'wrapped in foil' sits beside 'sandwiches', the thing actually wrapped

examples.text: She packed sandwiches for the hikers wrapped in foil.
examples.label: now the foil wraps the hikers

sections.tip: Read the full sentence once per slot. The right slot puts the word against its target; every other slot points it at something else.

sections.heading: The idiom hit-list
body: Practice these common pairings: make for, insight into, capable of, comply with, preoccupied with, different from.
For an underlined preposition, identify the governing verb or adjective and the intended meaning. Choose the standard construction for that use.

examples.text: Her interviews give insight into the engineers' decisions.
examples.label: 'insight' takes 'into'

examples.text: The drone is capable to fly in high winds.
examples.label: 'capable' takes 'of' + -ing: 'capable of flying'

examples.text: Preoccupied with checking the measurements, the team overlooked the delivery notice.
examples.label: Preoccupied with introduces what occupies the team’s attention.

sections.tip: Six pairs: make for, insight into, capable of, comply with, preoccupied with, different from. Say them until each sounds like one word.

sections.heading: Advanced transfer: prove meaning before using a shortcut
body: Before choosing, test the exact marked span. A replacement can duplicate an unchanged subject or verb, omit a limitation, or fail a second requirement in the question.
A colon follows a complete clause and introduces an explanation. Preserve the words and punctuation already outside the marked span.
For an evidence claim, retain the sample, measured outcome and uncertainty. A rating survey does not prove better performance or a result for everyone.

examples.text: Stem: 'The plan will help [[residents; it]] will cut fares.' Replacing the span with 'residents because it' makes one complete causal sentence.
examples.label: Only the marked words change; the following will is already supplied.

examples.text: Replacing the same span with 'residents because it will'.
examples.label: The complete sentence would say it will will cut fares; a correct phrase alone can still fail its context.

examples.text: The investigation established one fact: the two valves opened at different pressures.
examples.label: The complete introduction precedes a colon and a complete explanatory clause.

examples.text: Eighty volunteers rated the prototype; sixty found its controls easier to use. A precise conclusion is “Sixty volunteers reported that the controls were easier to use.”
examples.label: The conclusion preserves the surveyed group and the reported measure instead of claiming that everyone performed better.

sections.tip: Insert the exact words, reread the whole sentence, and explain the closest distractor’s error.

check.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence grammatically complete and correct?
check.stem: The passengers who used the station every day [[they]] remembered the old clock above the ticket office.
check.explanation: The full subject is The passengers who used the station every day. Deleting they lets that subject connect to remembered, the main verb. Who would start another dependent clause, and having would turn remembered into a nonfinite phrase; neither supplies the main predicate the subject needs.

check.questionText: Which choice most clearly identifies which dishes the seniors cooked and who taught them the recipes?
check.stem: At the heritage fair, the seniors cooked [[several traditional dishes they had learned to make]].
choices: dishes that drew one of the longest lines at the fair
tamales and pozole from recipes their grandmothers taught them
tamales and pozole that sold out within the first hour
food far more authentic than the usual fair offerings
check.explanation: 'tamales and pozole from recipes their grandmothers taught them' names the dishes and the teachers, meeting both requirements. 'tamales and pozole that sold out within the first hour' names only the dishes, and the other two choices name neither.

check.questionText: Which choice provides the most logical and grammatically correct connection between the two parts of the sentence?
check.stem: The greenhouse lost power overnight, [[but]] every seedling survived the cold.
check.explanation: Comma plus 'but' joins the clauses correctly and signals the surprise that the seedlings survived, so the original stands. 'nonetheless,' creates a comma splice, 'as a result,' splices the clauses and claims the power loss helped the seedlings, and deleting the word leaves a bare comma splice.
